title: The trains
hookLine: in 1947 trains of refugees crossed the new border, and violence struck on both sides

cards: A small railway station at night, beside a river, in a village where Sikhs and Muslims share the same fields and the same gossip. A train comes in from across the new border, and nobody gets off.
That's a scene from Train to Pakistan, a novel by the Sikh writer Khushwant Singh, set in the summer of 1947. The train is fiction. The trains behind it were not.
When the line between India and Pakistan was drawn, families who found themselves on the wrong side packed what they could carry and crowded onto trains going the other way.

teach.b: First, both directions. Hindus and Sikhs traveled east into India; Muslims traveled west into Pakistan. The same rails carried frightened people both ways, with children on laps and bundles on the roof.

teach.h: VIOLENCE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE LINE.
teach.b: Second, both sides of the line. Trains were attacked, and the killing was done by mobs on each side of the new border, to people on each side.

Sikhs suffered terribly in 1947, and some Sikhs also did terrible things to Muslim neighbors. Honest histories of Partition say this plainly, and so does Khushwant Singh's novel. Third, the hero of the story.
In the novel, men plan to stop a train of Muslims bound for Pakistan by stretching a rope across a bridge.
Jugga, a rough Sikh villager the police call a bad character, climbs up in the dark, cuts the rope, and is shot doing it. The train goes through.
A novelist who lived through that year chose to end his book with a Sikh giving his life for a train full of Muslims. Fourth, the old words.
At Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that since he found the company of the holy, he sees no one as an enemy and no one as a stranger, and he gets along with all.
And every Ardas ends by asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of our side. All.

how: Sikh families with Partition memories retell them at home and in the gurdwara, and the Ardas said at the close of every service asks for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

practice: Bring to mind the families on those trains, going east and going west, Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and the people on each platform waiting for someone who didn't come.

Don't sort them: breathe in and widen the circle, breathe out and leave no one outside it. If you pray, ask for sarbat da bhala, the good of all, the way the Ardas does; if you don't, simply wish them all well.

wordCard.voice: The trains. The crowded trains of 1947 that carried refugees both ways across the new border, and were attacked on both sides. Today's word.

orig.note: the good of all, asked for at the close of the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for every side. The good of all means all. See you tomorrow.
